strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reducing LLM inference cost by converting dense FFNs into sparse MoE architectures.
Proposes a training-free conversion pipeline with activation profiling, shared/routed expert grouping, balanced assignment clustering, and analytical router initialization.
The method is described clearly with equations and an overview figure, making the core procedure understandable.
Reports consistent improvements over LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 baselines in both training-free and LoRA fine-tuned settings across PPL and downstream tasks.
Provides a controllable performance-efficiency trade-off, showing a 1.5x end-to-end latency reduction at 25% activation and near-dense PPL at 75% activation.
Includes useful ablations on calibration data size, expert configuration, load balancing, and scaling to LLaMA-2 13B, plus a limitations discussion.
Demonstrates practical construction time under five minutes on a single GPU and shows that lightweight LoRA fine-tuning can recover substantial downstream performance.
Combines shared and routed experts with balanced assignment, which is a reasonable design for preserving common knowledge while enabling sparsity.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'lossless precision' at 75% activation with 5% acceleration is not supported by the reported results: Table 1 shows CMoE 75% training-free PPL 7.02 vs. dense 5.27 on Llama-2 7B, and after LoRA fine-tuning 5.69 vs. 5.27; on C4, 10.21 vs. 7.27, and on Llama-3 8B, 8.26 vs. 6.14 and 17.06 vs. 9.44, which is far from lossless.

The abstract's claim that a brief LoRA process recovers over 76% of dense downstream accuracy is ambiguous and, for the 25% configuration, is contradicted by Table 2: average recovery across six tasks is roughly 65%, with BoolQ 55.04/82.04 and ARC-C 27.56/53.15, not above 76%.

The training-free 25% configuration is not practically 'usable': PPL is 60.86 on WikiText-2 and 143.38 on Llama-3 8B, and zero-shot BoolQ is 46.09, below random, so the practical utility of the training-free setting is overstated.

The analytical router derivation is an approximation rather than a rigorous solution: it minimizes an expected-value surrogate and assumes representative hidden states approximate expected hidden states, which may yield weakly input-dependent or nearly static routing; no error bounds or formal guarantees are provided.

The hypothesis argmin |h_i w_down,i| ≈ argmin |h_i| is heuristic and may fail when down-projection magnitudes vary across neurons; the appendix only provides empirical histograms, not a theoretical or robustness analysis.

Baseline comparisons are limited to LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2; there is no comparison to MoEfication or other training-free dense-to-MoE conversion methods, and the very poor training-free baseline numbers raise questions about fair tuning of the baselines.

Inference speed evaluation is incomplete: no hardware details, absolute latency, batch size, memory usage, or routing overhead analysis are reported, and the 75% configuration achieves only about 1.05x full-model speedup, which is a weak efficiency gain.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL ('available at .'), lack of released code link, no error bars or significance tests, and limited reporting of evaluation prompts and fine-tuning details for downstream tasks.

The 'training-free' selling point is undermined by the fact that competitive downstream performance requires LoRA fine-tuning; the method still depends on calibration data and additional training to be useful.
Load balancing is only evaluated with an expert-load histogram, not with downstream task performance or PPL, so its practical effect on final model quality is unclear.

Writing and presentation need improvement: there are typos, grammar issues, inconsistent terminology, and abstract claims that do not align with the tables; some equations and table formatting are confusing.

strengths: Introduces a novel training-free framework for converting dense LLM FFNs into sparse MoE architectures, combining activation profiling, balanced assignment, and analytical router construction.

Provides an extensive empirical study across Llama-2 7B/13B and Llama-3 8B, covering perplexity, six downstream tasks, inference speed, and multiple ablations (calibration size, expert configuration, fine-tuning data, load balancing).
Outperforms LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 in both training-free and lightweight fine-tuned settings, showing clear practical gains over existing dense-to-MoE baselines.

Demonstrates a useful efficiency trade-off: 25% activation gives up to 1.5x end-to-end latency reduction, while 75% activation approaches dense-model downstream performance after brief LoRA fine-tuning.
The appendices add useful analyses on activation sparsity, calibration data size, and scaling to 13B models, supporting the plausibility of the approach.
weaknesses: The claim of 'lossless precision' at 75% activation is not supported by the reported results: WikiText-2 perplexity is 7.02 (training-free) and 5.69 (fine-tuned) versus 5.27 for the dense model, and C4 perplexity is 10.98/10.21 versus 7.27. This is a significant overstatement.

The abstract's claim that 25% activation 'preserves usable perplexity without additional training' is questionable: training-free PPL is about 60.86 on WikiText-2 and 135.61 on C4, far from usable for language modeling.

The abstract's statement that LoRA fine-tuning 'recovers over 76% of the dense model's downstream accuracy' is misleading for 25% activation. On several benchmarks the recovery is much lower (e.g., ARC-C ~52%, HellaSwag ~49%), and only SciQ clearly exceeds 76%; the text later narrows this to SciQ and BoolQ.

Inference speedup measurements lack essential details: GPU type, batch size, sequence length, implementation (e.g., sparse kernels or expert routing overhead), and latency measurement protocol are not specified. The 75% configuration reports only 1.02–1.05x full-model speedup, which may be within noise and has no variance estimate.

Reproducibility is weakened by a blank code URL ('available at .') and missing implementation details. The paper also does not explain how the large balanced assignment problem (roughly 9632x9632 for Llama-2 7B) is solved within the claimed five-minute conversion time.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair: LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 are designed for continual pre-training or post-training, so comparing them in a training-free state disadvantages them. The fine-tuned comparison helps, but other training-free conversion or pruning/quantization baselines are not evaluated.

There are no statistical significance tests or error bars across seeds, and performance appears sensitive to calibration data choice and size. This limits confidence in the robustness of the reported gains.

Some mathematical approximations in the router derivation (e.g., Eq. 3 and Eq. 13–19) are not fully justified across layers and models, and the quality of the analytically constructed router is evaluated only through end metrics, not directly.
The paper contains minor typographical and formatting issues (e.g., the title's 'Converting Mixture-of-Experts from Dense' is awkward, and a duplicated '12] modifies [12]' in Related Work).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely relevant and practically important problem for the NLP community: reducing the inference cost of large dense LLMs by restructuring FFN layers into sparsely activated MoE modules without full continued pre-training.

The conversion pipeline is described in sufficient algorithmic detail to be implementable in principle: ATopK profiling of FFN hidden states (Eq. 4), a shared/routed partition, a reduction of the constrained balanced K-means to a balanced linear-assignment problem (Eqs. 7-10), a router built from cluster representative neurons (Eqs. 17-19), and a differentiable/load-balanced variant (Sec. 3.3).

The empirical scope is wider than a single setting: two base model families (Llama-2 7B, Llama-3 8B, plus Llama-2 13B in the appendix), training-free and LoRA-fine-tuned regimes, perplexity on two corpora, six downstream benchmarks, latency measurements, and ablations on calibration size, expert configuration, and load balancing.

Latency is reported separately for memory-bound and compute-bound regimes (Table 3), which is the appropriate way to characterize MoE speedups; the reported ~1.5x end-to-end speedup at 25% activation is a plausible and meaningful efficiency gain.

The observation that FFN hidden-state values are sharply concentrated near zero (Fig. A.1) and the resulting cheap ATopK proxy are reasonable, and the inclusion of a training-free vs. LoRA-fine-tuned contrast plus a calibration-size ablation (Fig. 2, Table B.1) is useful for understanding the method's sensitivity.

Training-free results at 25% activation are clearly better than the training-free LLaMA-MoE / LLaMA-MoE-v2 baselines reported in Table 1, indicating that the analytical router initialization is at least more functional than a randomly initialized router.
weaknesses: The headline claim is contradicted by the paper's own results. The abstract, contributions bullet, and conclusion all state that at 75% activation CMoE delivers "lossless precision in terms of perplexity" while retaining a 5% speedup. Table 1 shows dense Llama-2 7B at 5.27 (WikiText-2) / 7.27 (C4) versus CMoE-75% at 7.02 / 10.98 training-free and 5.69 / 10.21 fine-tuned, and dense Llama-3 8B at 6.14 / 9.44 versus CMoE-75% fine-tuned at 8.26 / 17.06. These are 30-80% perplexity degradations, not lossless behavior. This is a central, repeated, and unsupported claim.

The "usable perplexity" claim for the training-free 25% configuration is also unsupported. 60.86 PPL (vs. 5.27 dense) is roughly an 11.5x degradation, and Table 2 shows that same training-free configuration at BoolQ 46.09 (below the ~62% majority baseline), ARC-C 23.80 (chance is 25%), and HellaSwag 38.79 (chance is 25%). The paper's core selling point (training-free conversion) therefore does not deliver a usable model on downstream tasks; nearly all competitive numbers require the LoRA stage.

The baseline comparison is unfair and effectively rigged. LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 are designed for continued pre-training / post-training, yet they are evaluated with a randomly initialized router in the "training-free" column (yielding NaN and >10k PPL) and then fine-tuned only with the authors' own LoRA recipe, which trains LoRA parameters and a scalar router scale but does not train the baselines' routers. Reporting 468.00 and 322.20 PPL for fine-tuned LLaMA-MoE is not a meaningful comparison to a method whose router is analytically initialized.

Calibration data is drawn from WikiText-2 while WikiText-2 is also a primary perplexity evaluation set, creating a domain-match/leakage advantage that the paper never controls for. The effect is large and visible (e.g., Llama-3 8B: 10.16 WikiText-2 vs. 17.35 C4 training-free), and Appendix C itself confirms that domain-matched calibration helps. The headline WikiText-2 numbers are therefore likely optimistic relative to the method's general behavior.

Reproducibility is incomplete in ways that matter for an efficiency paper. The code URL in the abstract is literally blank ("available at ."). Table 3 reports latency on "one single GPU" with no GPU model, batch size, or sequence length, and no details on how MoE kernels were implemented (dense masked computation vs. grouped GEMM), which determines whether the reported speedups are achievable in practice.

The methodological derivation has loose steps presented as exact. Eq. (3) claims argmin_i |h_i w_down,i| ≈ argmin_i |h_i|, but this ignores variation in the column norms of W_down; the paper normalizes X, W_gate and W_up in the appendix but never states that W_down is normalized, so the ATopK neuron ranking can be changed by rescaling W_down. Similarly, Eq. (19) equates a single-token representative-neuron activation with a calibration-set expected value, which is a heuristic, not an analytical solution to Eq. (12), despite the framing.

The paper never directly validates the fidelity of the conversion (e.g., reconstruction error between the MoE FFN output and the dense FFN output, or routing agreement with a full-activation oracle), which is the natural diagnostic for a conversion method and would clarify how much of the final performance comes from the construction versus the LoRA fine-tuning.

No random-partition or magnitude-pruning baseline at matched sparsity is provided in the main tables. Since the paper's argument is that activation-guided grouping and balanced assignment are what matter, the absence of a matched-sparsity control (other than LLaMA-MoE's random split, which is evaluated unfairly) leaves the source of the gains unclear.

Reporting is inconsistent and under-specified. Table 1's caption states activation ratios are varied at "fixed 1:1 shared/routed," yet Table 3 and Table 5 use configurations such as S1A3E16 and S2A2E16, which are not 1:1. The abstract/conclusion claim of recovering ">76% of the dense model's downstream accuracy" is never defined (relative to which tasks, which metric, which configuration), and the per-task ratios in Table 2 range from ~49% to ~92%.

The definition of the expert score is internally contradictory. Eq. (11) fixes g_i ∈ {0,1} "to enable an un-scaled version of the expert output," and Sec. 3.3 immediately redefines g_i = 1 + s'_i·u_i (a real-valued, scaled gate). The claim of avoiding bias therefore does not hold once the differentiable variant is introduced.

The writing and typesetting contain numerous errors that suggest insufficient proofreading: the missing code URL; "[12] modifies [12] modifies the LLaMA-2 7B model"; "SliceGPT [26] substitutes each weight matrix with a smaller dense matrix oo deease the embedding dimension"; "the output of original output of the dense FFN"; "substituting each weight matrix...". Table 1's TF/FT column layout is also confusing.

Novelty relative to MoEfication (Zhang et al., 2021) and the LLaMA-MoE line is incremental: co-activation clustering of FFN neurons plus a hidden-state-based router is the established recipe, and the new elements (balanced-assignment formulation, representative-neuron router initialization, DeepSeek-V3-style bias load balancing, LoRA adaptation) are largely combinations of existing components. The paper does not analyze which component drives the improvements.

There are no multiple-seed runs, variance estimates, or significance tests anywhere, and the comparisons are frequently within a few points (e.g., S1A1E8 vs. S2A2E16 in Table 5), so several conclusions in the ablation are not supported at the precision claimed.

strengths: Introduces a simple and practical post-training method to convert dense FFNs into sparse MoE architectures using activation pattern analysis, with shared experts for high-frequency neurons and routed experts for conditionally active neurons.

Provides a training-free analytical router construction with optional lightweight LoRA fine-tuning, significantly reducing resource requirements (4M tokens, minutes of construction) compared to prior MoE restructuring methods that use billions of tokens.

Extensive experiments on multiple models (Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-30B-A3B, Qwen-2.5-72B) and benchmarks, including ablations for clustering/routing, calibration sensitivity, token budget, FLOPs/throughput, load balancing, orthogonality with activation sparsity, and self-consistency.

Consistently outperforms prior MoE restructuring and structured pruning baselines at matched 2k-sample fine-tuning budgets in zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, with training-free performance often close to fine-tuned performance.
Well-written and organized, with clear motivation, figures, and an honest limitations section.
weaknesses: The inference speedup is modest (up to 1.17x in compute-bound 32k-context settings, around 1.1x otherwise), and accuracy still trails dense baselines by a notable margin, which may limit practical deployment impact.

The comparison against resource-heavy baselines such as LLaMA-MoE-v2 is based on reimplemented versions fine-tuned with only 2k samples, not their full-scale pretraining budgets; this may understate those methods' potential and weakens the claim of outperforming them.
No statistical significance or variance is reported across random seeds, calibration sets, or runs; most results appear to be single-run, making it difficult to assess robustness.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, hardware details for time/speed measurements are not specified, and some methodological details (e.g., how multiple shared experts are combined, exact expert partition sizes) are ambiguous.

Calibration/domain robustness is only partially evaluated; the paper shows activation overlap across domains but does not measure downstream performance under domain shift, despite relying on calibration data.

The analytical router derivation relies on approximations (e.g., using L1 hidden-state magnitude as a proxy for reconstruction error) without formal guarantees, and the theoretical analysis is limited.
Evaluation is restricted to English decoder-only models; multilingual, encoder-decoder, and other architectures are left to future work, limiting generality.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: post-training FFN-to-MoE restructuring for efficient LLM inference without expensive pretraining.

The method is simple and well-motivated by empirical analysis: activation profiling reveals bimodal neuron activation frequencies, leading to a clean separation of always-active shared experts and conditionally active routed experts.

Strong and broad empirical evaluation across four models (Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-30B-A3B) and multiple benchmarks, with consistent improvements over MoE restructuring and structured pruning baselines.

Extensive analyses and ablations cover training-free vs fine-tuned performance, calibration sensitivity, clustering/routing choices, token budgets, FLOPs/throughput, load balancing, orthogonality with activation sparsity, expert configurations, and self-consistency.

Practical efficiency is demonstrated: 4.5-minute analytical construction, 2k-sample fine-tuning, up to 1.17x speedup, 16.6% FLOPs reduction, and 14.8% throughput gain, with compatibility with other efficiency techniques.
Clear writing and good reproducibility details, including model names, hyperparameters, calibration data, LoRA settings, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is not fully convincing: LLaMA-MoE/v2 and EMoE are reimplemented and fine-tuned with only 2k samples, while their original training uses orders of magnitude more tokens; the claim of outperforming full-resource methods is therefore not directly supported.

Qwen-3-30B-A3B is an MoE model, but Tables 1 and 7 label its original baseline as "Dense"; this mislabeling obscures whether the comparison is against the original MoE routing or an all-experts-active version.

The theoretical derivation is heuristic rather than rigorous: the reduction of reconstruction error to L1 hidden-state magnitude (Eqs. 22-23) relies on approximations and a sparsity hypothesis, and L1 hidden magnitude may not faithfully proxy expert output magnitude when down-projection weights vary.

The analytical router uses a single representative neuron per routed expert, which is a coarse approximation for experts containing hundreds or thousands of neurons; sensitivity to this choice and its theoretical justification are limited.

Main experiments use only 25% FFN sparsity (75% active neurons), a mild regime; efficiency gains are modest (up to 1.17x), and MoE baselines may not be operating in their natural sparse regime, limiting conclusions about practical acceleration.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and some hyperparameters (K_a=10, shared/routed expert counts, calibration size) are set without systematic justification; results appear to be single runs without variance or error bars.
Evaluation is limited to English decoder-only models; multilingual and encoder-decoder/state-space architectures are left to future work, which limits generalizability.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a coherent pipeline from activation profiling to expert construction and router design.

The proposed post-training framework is practically appealing: it requires only a small calibration set (8 examples, 2048 tokens each) and optional lightweight LoRA fine-tuning, making it accessible for resource-constrained settings.

The experiments are broad, covering Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5 7B, and Qwen-3-30B-A3B across five zero-shot tasks plus MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, and include multiple ablations (clustering vs routing, expert configuration, calibration sensitivity, orthogonality with WINA).

The training-free variant already achieves competitive results (e.g., 42.50 MMLU on Llama-2 7B) and even outperforms some fine-tuned baselines, suggesting the analytical router initialization has merit.
The efficiency analysis is useful: it reports FLOPs, MACs, throughput, load balancing, and compatibility with quantization and neuron-level activation sparsity.
The method is orthogonal to several existing efficiency techniques and can be composed with them, which is a practically valuable property.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method outperforms prior MoE restructuring methods requiring orders of magnitude more resources is not adequately supported. Baselines such as LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and EMoE are reimplemented and fine-tuned with only 2k samples, even though they were designed for continual pretraining with 200B/7B tokens. The paper then compares its 4M-token pipeline to the reported resource requirements of those baselines, but does not actually train them under those conditions. This is an unfair and misleading comparison.

The analytical router construction is not theoretically justified. The objective in Section 3.3 requires ranking experts by expected hidden-state magnitude, but the router is built from a representative neuron chosen by binary activation-pattern similarity to a cluster centroid. There is no proof or empirical validation that this representative neuron's hidden activation approximates the expert's expected output contribution or solves the reconstruction error objective.

The key activation bimodality observation is not validated under the experimental setting. Figure 2 uses K_a=1000 for visualization, while the main experiments use K_a=10. The caption claims similar patterns hold at smaller K_a, but no evidence is provided. If the bimodal separation does not hold at K_a=10, the shared/routed expert partition may be unfounded.

The empirical gains are often small and reported without variance or significance testing. For example, PIQA improves from 73.13 to 74.34 over SLEB on Llama-2 7B, and throughput gains are around 14-15% in most settings. Single-run numbers make it difficult to assess whether improvements are robust.

The efficiency gains are modest: 16.6% FLOPs reduction and 14.8% throughput improvement on Llama-2 7B, with the headline 1.17x speedup only in a specific compute-bound 32k-context setting. This may not justify the added complexity of the MoE restructuring pipeline.

Novelty is limited. Shared experts, activation-based neuron clustering, and analytical router construction are all related to existing work; the contribution is primarily a combination and engineering of known ideas. The paper does not sufficiently isolate which component drives the gains beyond the existing MoEfication/G-MoEfication/READ-ME comparisons.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a code release or detailed implementation artifacts. Key design choices, such as how the number of shared vs routed experts is selected, how the balanced clustering is tuned, and how calibration examples are sampled, are not fully specified.

The evaluation is limited to English benchmarks and decoder-only transformer models. While the limitations section acknowledges this, the paper's broad claims about LLM acceleration would benefit from at least some multilingual or encoder-decoder validation.
